After a job loss: chart the settlement date, the income gap and the cash runway

Use four interactive graphics to map eighteen months of receipts and spending, compare a temporary budget reduction and expose cash gaps before later money arrives.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore an 18-month job-loss cash calendar

Interactive planning lab

Additional starting cash needed, with the reduction$0
First unfunded point, with the reductionNone in 18 months
Cash after month 18, with the reduction$29,000

Original hypothetical 18-month cash ledger. Immediate transition costs are paid at time zero. All monthly receipts arrive at the start of their labeled month, before that month’s spending. Continuing net income remains throughout; new net earnings are additional. Temporary support begins after the entered full delay, lasts at most the entered payment count and stops when new earnings start. There is no catch-up payment for delayed months. One net settlement is received in its independently entered month regardless of work status. The spending reduction applies only before new earnings begin and cannot make spending negative. Accessible cash earns zero. No EI eligibility, statutory amount, waiting period, severance allocation, tax, benefit coordination, legal entitlement, credit facility or investment sale is calculated. Negative cash represents an unfunded requirement, not a permitted overdraft.

The central idea

A settlement amount needs a receipt date. Build the transition reserve from the lowest cash point, then review the budget again when temporary support ends or new earnings begin.

01

Start with accessible cash and confirmed net receipts

The first number in a job-loss budget is the cash that can actually pay the next bill. Separate accessible savings from locked deposits, securities that would have to be sold, an expected settlement and unused borrowing capacity. They have different receipt dates, conditions and consequences. Do not add an undrawn credit limit to savings without also modeling the resulting debt.

This example starts with CAD 18,000 of accessible cash and pays CAD 1,000 of transition costs before month one. Its opening chart point is therefore CAD 17,000. A separately entered CAD 12,000 settlement arrives at the start of month two. It is not available at time zero.

Use amounts expected to reach the bank account after relevant deductions and any independently assessed obligations. Keep the gross settlement document beside a separate receipt estimate. The FCAC job-loss guide provides general context for reviewing compensation, spending and available savings. The calculator determines none of those entitlements.

02

Put each recurring receipt on its own timeline

The default household retains CAD 1,500 of other monthly net income. Temporary support of CAD 1,800 begins in month three, after two full months without it, and lasts for six payments. New earnings of CAD 4,200 begin in month ten, in addition to the continuing CAD 1,500.

That creates three distinct income windows. Months one and two have CAD 1,500 of recurring income; months three through eight have CAD 3,300; month nine falls back to CAD 1,500. From month ten, recurring receipts become CAD 5,700. The one-off settlement stays outside these recurring-income bars.

The assumed support schedule is an independent net cash input. It is not an EI calculation, a promise of approval or a statutory payment window. Delaying its start moves the entire modeled payment window; it does not create an arrears cheque. If new earnings begin sooner, the example stops support at that point. Real arrangements may behave differently and need a separately confirmed schedule.

03

Give the spending reduction a start and an end

Normal spending is CAD 4,500 per month. The selected CAD 600 reduction lowers it to CAD 3,900 before new earnings begin. The model restores normal spending from month ten. This avoids quietly assuming that an emergency budget will remain achievable for the next eighteen months.

During the first two months, recurring income is CAD 2,400 below the reduced budget. During the six support months, the gap is CAD 600 per month. Month nine returns to a CAD 2,400 gap. From month ten onward, the normal budget has a CAD 1,200 monthly surplus under the chosen receipts.

A workable reduction needs named expenses and realistic cancellation dates. Required loan payments, insurance and basic housing costs may be less flexible than travel or optional subscriptions. The control caps spending at zero if the entered reduction exceeds the normal budget; it does not treat an unused reduction as new income. New work-related expenses should be included in the normal budget or assessed separately.

04

A positive ending balance can hide an earlier shortage

The default reduced-budget path ends month eighteen with CAD 29,000 and stays funded throughout. That result depends on receiving the settlement in month two. Change accessible cash to CAD 3,000 and the settlement month to six while retaining the other defaults. The ending balance is still positive, but the cash position falls below zero before the settlement arrives.

In that timing stress, cash after the immediate cost is CAD 2,000. It falls to negative CAD 400 after month one and reaches negative CAD 4,600 after month five. The additional starting reserve needed to prevent every modeled shortage is CAD 4,600. The later CAD 12,000 receipt cannot retroactively pay an earlier bill.

The reserve calculation takes the largest cumulative deficit, including the immediate cost at time zero. Negative values identify funding that has not been arranged. The line does not approve an overdraft, assume a creditor will wait or calculate interest on borrowing that might bridge the gap.

05

Use the four graphics together

The income bars explain recurring receipts. The cash lines show what happens after the entire receipt and spending calendar, with and without the temporary reduction. The waterfall reconciles the final balance by counting the settlement once, eighteen months of continuing income, support actually received, new earnings actually received and all modeled costs.

The matrix changes the first new-earnings month and settlement month. It holds the existing reserve and other assumptions fixed, then recalculates the extra starting cash needed for each timing combination. Its rows are job-search stresses, without probabilities. A later job start can also extend the period with reduced spending, so each cell must rerun the whole ledger.

All monthly receipts are assumed to arrive before that month’s spending. Rent due before a late-month receipt could require more cash than these month-end balances show. For an immediate decision, replace the monthly calendar with actual paydays, bill dates and confirmed processing times.

06

Build a review calendar for the transition

  1. Reconcile current accessible balances and immediate transition bills.
  2. Confirm the amount and expected receipt date of every one-off payment.
  3. Record support as a separate schedule, with an end date and any conditions.
  4. Identify feasible spending changes and when normal spending resumes.
  5. Stress a later first paycheque and check the lowest cash point.
  6. After employment resumes, review reserve rebuilding and any remaining debt.

The official EI regular-benefits page is the starting point for current application and qualification information. Consult the relevant authority about how actual earnings and settlement terms affect a claim. This tool excludes benefit coordination, tax reconciliation, investment sales and employment-law advice. Update the ledger as dates become confirmed rather than using a large final settlement to dismiss a near-term cash gap.
